items.title: Beyond Instruction Override: Benchmarking Indirect Prompt Injection with Task-Tampering Attacks
items.summary_1line: Indirect prompt-injection (IPI) benchmarks predominantly test planted instructions that redirect a tool-using agent toward an attacker-chosen task. Yet attacker-controlled content can instead tamper with the outcome o...
items.editor_note: Benchmark for attacks that tamper with task outcomes rather than override instructions.

editorial.tldr: Late October papers proposed model-level defenses: learned attention gates (Heads of Security) and adversarial training (SecPO). Early November papers then widened the attack surface to persistent agent memory and silently updated tools.
editorial.whats_new: A new benchmark shows indirect prompt injection can tamper with a tool-using agent's task outcome rather than just redirect it, a case most IPI benchmarks do not test.
editorial.why_it_matters: Defenses tuned to block instruction override can miss attacks that corrupt memory, tool updates, or task results; test those paths before trusting a guardrail.
editorial.take_for_builders: Add a task-tampering case, a cross-session memory-poisoning case, and a tool-version-change check to your agent red-team suite, and do not rely on instruction-override tests alone.

status.detail: Research is shifting from single-turn instruction override to memory, tool-update, and task-tampering attacks, with new runtime defenses alongside.

beats.headline: Attention gates and adversarial training target injection robustness
beats.summary: Heads of Security enforces instruction-data separation with learned per-head attention gates; SecPO proposes principled adversarial training.

beats.headline: Persistent memory and tool updates open gaps beyond single-session injection
beats.summary: MemHarmBench tests cross-session injection in memory-persistent agents; the Tool Update Gap paper shows frameworks may keep trusting tools after updates.

beats.headline: SPILLWAY separates target admission from sanitization
beats.summary: Argues against putting an LLM on the decision that lets an action through, since that decision can itself be manipulated.

beats.headline: Task-tampering benchmark exposes a gap in IPI evaluation
beats.summary: Attacker-controlled content can alter the outcome of the user's task instead of redirecting the agent.

open_questions: Do learned attention gates (Heads of Security) and SecPO training hold up against task-tampering attacks?
Do the memory and tool-update attack papers ship reproducible harnesses that independent teams can run?
Does SPILLWAY's admission/sanitization split keep its robustness in independent evaluation on real agent frameworks?
